r0060: 1.  Independence and impartiality of the National Security Court (*cour de sûreté de l’Etat*)
r0061: 27.  The Government submitted, firstly, that the presence of a military judge on a court alongside civilian judges did not in itself amount to a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. In support of their argument, they referred to the Court’s case-law (among others, the judgments in Engel and Others v. the Netherlands, Belilos v. Switzerland and Campbell and Fell v. the United Kingdom).
r0062: 28.  The Government also submitted that the constitutional provisions governing the appointment of judges, the legislation on military judges sitting in national security courts (*cours de sûreté de l’Etat*) and the guarantees enjoyed by the latter in the performance of their judicial duties were such that those courts fully complied with the requirement of independence and impartiality laid down in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.
r0063: 29.  The Government further pointed out that on 18 June 1999 Article 143 of the Constitution, governing the composition of national security courts (*cours de sûreté de l’Etat*), had been amended. They submitted in particular that, following that amendment, Law no. 4390 now provided that the duties of military judges and prosecutors would end on 22 June 1999. The Government concluded that the applicant could not have any legal interest in his complaint of a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.
r0064: 30.  The applicant disputed the Government’s argument. Referring to the judgment in Incal v. Turkey of 9 June 1998 (Reports 1998-IV, § 72), he submitted that the National Security Court (*cour de sûreté de l’Etat*) before which he had been tried and convicted could not be regarded as an “independent and impartial tribunal” within the meaning of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant further stressed that the constitutional and legislative amendments concerning the status of national security courts could have no bearing on his situation, since the Istanbul National Security Court, which had heard his case and convicted him on 4 March 1997, had at that time been composed of three judges, one of whom was a military judge.
r0065: 31.  The Court reiterates that in Incal v. Turkey (cited above) and Çıraklar v. Turkey (cited above) it has already examined complaints similar to those raised in the present case. In those cases the Court noted, in particular, that certain aspects of the status of military judges sitting as members of national security courts (*cours de sûreté de l’Etat*) made their independence and impartiality questionable (see Incal v. Turkey, cited above, p. 1571, § 68). It pointed out that the judges in question were servicemen who still belonged to the army, which in turn took its orders from the executive; that they remained subject to military discipline and that assessment reports were compiled on them by the army for that purpose; that decisions pertaining to their appointment were to a great extent taken by the administrative authorities and the army; and, lastly, that their term of office as national security court judges was four years and could be renewed.
r0066: 32.  The Court nevertheless takes into consideration the information provided by the Government according to which Turkish legislation has been amended so as to comply with the requirements of the Convention. However, it points out that its task is confined to assessing the particular circumstances of the case; it cannot therefore be called upon to find that a case no longer presents a valid legal interest for the applicant on the ground that developments have occurred in domestic legislation since the relevant time (see Sadak and Others v. Turkey, judgment of 17 July 2001, § 38).
r0067: 33.  It must therefore determine whether the applicant objectively had a legitimate reason to fear a lack of independence and impartiality on the part of the court which tried him (see İncal, cited above, p. 1572, § 70, and Çıraklar, cited above, p. 3072, § 38).
r0068: In that connection, the Court sees no reason to depart from the conclusion it reached in respect of Mr İncal and Mr Çıraklar, both of whom, like the applicant, were civilians. It is understandable in the present case that the applicant – who was being tried in a national security court (*cour de sûreté de l’Etat*) on a charge of having attempted to overthrow the Turkish constitutional order by force, an offence under Article 146 § 1 of the Criminal Code (*code pénal*) – should have been apprehensive about being tried by a bench which included a regular army officer who was a member of the military judiciary. On that account he could legitimately fear that the Istanbul National Security Court might allow itself to be unduly influenced by considerations which had nothing to do with the nature of his case. Accordingly, the applicant’s doubts about the independence and impartiality of that court may be regarded as objectively justified (see İncal, cited above, p. 1573, § 72 in fine).
